question: What is the meaning of ce declaration of performance in relation to sustainability performance, certificates, performance statements?
description: The CE declaration of performance in relation to sustainability performance, certificates, and performance statements refers to a declaration made by manufacturers to confirm that their products meet the essential requirements of the European Union (EU) for safety, health, and environmental protection. This declaration is part of the broader CE marking system, which allows products to circulate freely within the EU market. The declaration of performance includes information about the product's characteristics, performance, and compliance with EU standards, which can be used to assess the product's sustainability performance. Certificates and performance statements are often included in the declaration of performance to provide evidence of the product's compliance with specific standards or to validate certain aspects of the product's performance. These documents can be used by stakeholders, such as consumers, regulators, and certification bodies, to verify the product's sustainability credentials and ensure that it meets the required environmental and safety standards.

Article 17
General principles and use of CE marking
1.
The CE marking shall be subject to the general principles set out in Article 30 of Regulation (EC) No 765/2008.
2.
The CE marking shall be affixed only to those products for which the manufacturer has drawn up a declaration of 
performance and conformity in accordance with Articles 13 and 15. The CE marking shall be affixed to key parts.
3.
By affixing the CE marking to the product, or having it affixed, the economic operator indicates that it has assumed 
responsibility for the conformity of the product with the declared performance and applicable product requirements laid 
down in accordance with this Regulation. By affixing the CE marking, the economic operator becomes liable for the 
declared performance and the fulfilment of those requirements in accordance with national law on contractual and 
extra-contractual liability.
4.
The CE marking shall be the only marking attesting to the performance of the product with regard to assessed 
essential characteristics in accordance with this Regulation, as well as to the conformity of the product with this Regulation.
Article 18
Rules and conditions for the affixing of CE marking
1.
The CE marking shall be affixed visibly, legibly and indelibly to the product. Where this is not possible or not 
warranted on account of the nature of the product, the CE marking shall be affixed to a label attached to the product or to 
the packaging or, where that is also not possible, to the accompanying documents.
2.
The CE marking shall be followed by:
(a) the last two digits of the year in which the CE marking was first affixed; or, in the case of used products, the last two 
digits of the year when the product was deinstalled followed by the last two digits of the year in which the CE marking 
was affixed to the used product;
(b) the name and the registered address, or the identifying mark allowing easy and unambiguous identification of the name 
and address, of the manufacturer;
(c) the name and the registered address of the authorised representative, or the identifying mark allowing easy and 
unambiguous identification of the name and address of the authorised representative where the manufacturer does not 
have a place of business in the Union or where the manufacturer chooses to have an authorised representative;
(d) the unique identification code of the product-type;
(e) the declaration code of the declaration of performance and conformity;
(f) the identification number of the notified body or bodies verifying the product type and assessing the factory production 
control, if applicable; and
(g) a data carrier connected to the digital product passport referred to in Article 76 if such a digital product passport is 
available through the construction digital product passport system established pursuant to Article 75.
The information listed in points (d) and (e) of the first subparagraph of this paragraph may be replaced by a data carrier, 
including permalink connected to the declaration of performance and conformity pursuant to Article 16(2), point (e), if the 
declaration of performance and conformity is available on a website. The information listed in points (d) and (e) of the first 
subparagraph of this paragraph may be omitted if a data carrier referred to in point (g) of the first subparagraph of this 
paragraph is provided.
3.
The CE marking shall be affixed before the product is placed on the market. It may be followed by a pictogram or any 
other mark indicating a special risk or use.

The internationally recognized and accepted classification system for 
labels is issued by the ISO 14020 standard and categorizes labels into 
three types based on their verification (ISO, 2021b), self declarations 
(ISO, 2021a), and LCA data (ISO, 2021c). Eco-certificates and 
eco-labels frequently coincide, hence, the terms are often ’incor­
rectly’ used interchangeably to refer to the combination of concepts 
while concepts technically can exist independently. 
The key difference between certificates is that (1) an eco-certificate 
displays the environmental performance of a product on a static 
collected life cycle inventory while passport is a dynamic registration 
that takes place during the life cycle of a product, (2) not necessarily, but 
typically an eco-certificate is assigned to a product design, rather than a 
unique object, and (3) a passport attempts to valuate a product. 
3.6. Contents 
Passports appear in variants, for instance, with a focus on specific 
type of objects (e.g., buildings (Debacker and Manshoven, 2016), in­
frastructures (Wittenveen & Bos, 2018), clothing (Riedelsheimer et al., 
2020)) or with a specific purpose (e.g., renovation (Sesana et al., 2021), 
recycling (Spengler and Schr¨oter, 2003), optimizing operational use (Ye 
et al., 2020)). Passport requirements typically shape along with the 
intended product application. For example, a passport of a large com­
mercial company structure may not need the same level of detail as one 
for small residential buildings (Gonçalves et al., 2021; Transitieteam 
CBE, 2020; Wittenveen & Bos, 2018). Fig. 5 provides an overview of the 
attributes (lower level) that passports can typically consist of. This sup­
ports in deriving more holistic understanding of the typical components 
(higher-level) of a concept (bold text in Fig. 5 or see Fig. A4 and Table A6 
in Appendix A4). 
Nearly every passport contains a digital representation of the phys­
ical composition and technical characteristics of an object (C.12). 
Frequently reported data attributes are: information regarding the 
quality conditions of an object (C.1), the servicing history of an object 
(C.20), guidelines for maintenance, safety and recycling (C.13-C.18) and 
the valuation of an object (C.3). Performance indicators are also 
commonly part of a passport, but not all passports offer such metrics to 
measure the environmental performance of the object. EPDs and energy 
certificates are most frequently observed. Remarkable is the usual lack 
of circularity indicators (Moraga et al., 2019) reported while these align 
well with one of the key passport goals. A possible explanation is that 
sustainability and circularity indicators may introduce subjectivity both 
by focusing on specific aspects of sustainability or circularity and can 
apply weight to the objective results in selected indicator formula’s 
(Moraga et al., 2019). Moreover, for the sole purpose of identifying the 
value for use, recovery, and reuse, indicators may be helpful, but not 
always strictly required. There are two popular decision support attri­
butes in passports. Firstly, tools to explore options for recovery and 
renovation (C.49) which support object governance by letting users’ 
compare known alternative treatments. Secondly, scenario modelling 
(C.50) allows users to reason about unknown future states of the object 
which may help to identify a CE governance strategy. 
3.7. Stakeholders 
Since passports are about the governance of the entire product life 
cycle, it may be helpful to understand who the involved actors are, what 
their role is and perspective they hold toward passports. We choose to 
anchor the actor analysis to the most frequently used life cycle variant 
(Stark, 2015, p. 7).
